'''''Quercus pyrenaica''''', also known as '''Pyrenean oak''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> or '''Spanish oak'''<ref>{{cite web |title=Ageing in Spanish Oak |date=24 February 2020 |url=https://bodegaslan.com/en/ageing-in-spanish-oak/ |publisher=Bodegas LAN |access-date=21 June 2023 |archive-date=21 June 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230621170702/https://bodegaslan.com/en/ageing-in-spanish-oak/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> is a tree native to southwestern [[Europe]] and northwestern [[North Africa]]. Despite its common name, it is rarely found in the [[Pyrenees Mountains]] and is more abundant in northern Portugal and north and northwestern Spain.

It is placed in [[Quercus sect. Quercus|section ''Quercus'']].<ref>{{Citation |last1=Denk |first1=Thomas |last2=Grimm |first2=Guido W. |last3=Manos |first3=Paul S. |last4=Deng |first4=Min |last5=Hipp |first5=Andrew L. |date=2017-11-02 |title=Appendix 2.1: An updated infrageneric classification of the oaks |website=figshare |doi=10.6084/m9.figshare.5547622.v1 |url=https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/Appendix_2_1_________An_updated_infrageneric_classification_of_the_oaks/5547622/1 |access-date=2023-02-17 |format=xls |name-list-style=amp |mode=cs1}}</ref>

The oak is cultivated as an [[ornamental tree]] for gardens and parks.<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" />

==Description==
''Quercus pyrenaica'' is a tall [[deciduous]] tree, often [[marcescence|marcescent]] in immature individuals,<ref name="flora-on">{{cite web |title=Quercus pyrenaica Willd. |url=https://flora-on.pt/#/1quercus+pyrenaica |publisher=Flora-on |access-date=22 January 2021}}</ref> up to {{convert|25|m|ft|round=5|abbr=off}} tall, though it is sometimes found as a bush or small tree. It has an average lifespan of 300 years.<ref name=iucneurope>{{Cite iucn |title=''Quercus pyrenaica'' in Europe |author=Harvey-Brown, Y. |name-list-style=amp |article-number=e.T78972170A80570544 |date=2017 |access-date=22 January 2021}}</ref> The [[leaves]] have short petioles and are deeply and irregularly lobed, with four to eight pairs of lobes per leaf. There are stellate hairs on both sides of the leaf.<ref name="iberica">{{cite web |title=Quercus pyrenaica |url=http://www.floraiberica.es/floraiberica/texto/pdfs/02_041_03_Quercus.pdf |publisher=[[Flora Iberica]] |access-date=22 January 2021}}</ref> Roots frequently produce [[sucker (botany)|suckers]]. The species has high resprouting capabilities.<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" />

==Distribution and habitat==
''Quercus pyrenaica'' is native to the [[Iberian Peninsula]] and parts of southwest France and northern Morocco inhabiting mainly subatlantic or continental environments up to {{convert|2100|m|ft|sigfig=2|abbr=on}} in elevation.<ref name="iberica" /> In the Iberian Peninsula, which represents 95% of its population,<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" /> it occupies mainly the northern portion, south of the [[Cantabrian Mountains]], very common in the west of the Peninsula in the northern half of mountainous Portugal,<ref name="flora-on" /> and rare on the east<ref name="iberica" /> It is adapted both to sub-humid temperate and Mediterranean semi-arid conditions, from the humid [[Peneda-Gerês National Park]] in Portugal, to the semi-arid Spanish central plain. It is also adapted to survive in hot local temperatures. It is thought to have a short growth season to avoid the summer drought.<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" /> It is often the dominant species in the forests in which it occurs.<ref name=iucneurope /> Its acorns are dispersed by birds and small mammals.<ref name=iucneurope />

==Threats==
[[File:Quercus pyrenaica patológico 20090813 2.jpg|thumb|left|upright|Specimen affected by pathogens]]

The species is currently threatened by wild fire which encourage the growth of other oak species that ''Q. pyrenaica'' is unable to compete with, and insect pathogens such as green oak leaf roller moth (''[[Tortrix viridana]]''), the gipsy moth (''[[Lymantria dispar]]'') and [[brown-tail moth]] (''Euproctis chrysorrhoea''); these threats may become of greater concern due to the impact of climate change.<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" />

Historically the species experienced decline due to charcoal and timber industry, and forestry activities still pose some threat to ''Q. pyrenaica'' but on a much reduced scale.<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" />
